2.2.6.4-f10.accuracy_reason: Tusc. 3.41 reports Epicurus on the pleasant motions the eyes take from beautiful forms. The note's 'loosely echoes' is suitably hedged.

2.2.6.4-f18.accuracy_reason: Horace Sat. 2.1.71–74 begins 'Quin ubi se a vulgo', and 'illo' there is Lucilius.

2.2.6.4-f2.accuracy_reason: The Regimen Sanitatis Salernitanum names three 'doctors': 'mens laeta, requies, moderata diaeta'. The variant the note reports is correct.

2.2.6.4-f20.accuracy_reason: In Machiavelli's Life of Castruccio, Castruccio does say that one held wise by day will not be held a fool by night. The note is also right that Burton's English softens the saying.

2.2.6.4-f21.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 4.12.27 is right; the next line is 'dulce est desipere in loco'.

2.2.6.4-f22.accuracy_reason: Martial 11.104 reads 'Laida nocte volo'. The note is right that Burton has put in Thais.

2.2.6.4-f23.accuracy_reason: Plutarch, Lycurgus 25, records a statue of Laughter (Gelos) set up by Lycurgus. Apuleius' festival of Risus at Hypata in Thessaly is real, and the note hedges where the sidenote belongs.

2.2.6.4-f32.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.6.65–66 does read 'Mimnermus uti censet'.

2.2.6.4-f34.accuracy_reason: In the myth, Jupiter stretched his night with Alcmena to three nights' length, and Hercules was conceived.

2.2.6.4-f35.accuracy_reason: 'Pergraecari' does mean to revel Greek-fashion. Plautus, Mostellaria 22–23, has 'dies noctesque bibite, pergraecamini'.

2.2.6.4-f4.accuracy_reason: Publilius Syrus' sententia does read 'Comes facundus in via pro vehiculo est'.

2.2.6.4-f40.accuracy_reason: The proverb is correct, and Cicero gives it in Latin at Tusculan Disputations 5.118 as 'aut bibat aut abeat'.

2.2.6.4-f5.accuracy_reason: Satyricon 1 has 'mellitos verborum globulos' in its attack on the declaimers.

2.2.6.4-f60.accuracy_reason: Ad Familiares 7.22 reads 'etsi domum bene potus seroque redieram', and the suggested corruption is hedged.

2.2.6.4-f64.accuracy_reason: The Simonidean epitaph on Timocreon (Anth. Pal. 7.348) runs 'having eaten much, drunk much, and spoken much ill of men, here I lie, Timocreon of Rhodes'. The Latin renders its opening.

2.2.6.4-f65.accuracy_reason: Euripides, Andromache 930: Hermione says that the visits of wicked women ruined her. The Latin version is correct.
